curriculum.lesson_evidence: At the end of a drama unit, students share their best scene and reflect on what they learned. A performance review looks at role, voice, body, use of space, props and audience connection. Give feedback as two stars, which are things that worked well, and a wish, which is one change. A reflection names what you did well, what was challenging and what you will practise next. Treat every performer with respect, and speak about the performance rather than the person.
curriculum.scope_limit: Single lesson: partial evidence. Cross-check existing card mapping and NESA content point. Official wording for MA2-RN-01 is recorded in lesson-pipeline/sources/nesa-ma2-rn-01.json where applicable.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Write two stars and a wish about a scene you saw or performed this unit, using a drama term in each.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 'Star: the narrator's clear voice told the story well. Star: the kneeling level showed the sad character. Wish: use a prop to show where the cave is.' Each comment names a drama element and is about the performance.

WATCH FOR
Thinking that feedback should only say what was wrong. Good feedback names what worked, which tells the performer what to keep, and gives one clear idea to improve.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Prepare your best scene from the unit and perform it for family. Ask them for two stars and a wish using the words role, voice, body, space or prop. Write a reflection of five sentences about your strengths and a next step.

Write a short reflection naming one artistic choice you changed and why. Movement or instrument work is optional, adult-supervised and can be described instead.

WORKED MODEL

teach_steps.explain:
At the end of a drama unit, students share their best scene and reflect on what they learned. A performance review looks at role, voice, body, use of space, props and audience connection. Give feedback as two stars, which are things that worked well, and a wish, which is one change. A reflection names what you did well, what was challenging and what you will practise next. Treat every performer with respect, and speak about the performance rather than the person.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the elements, techniques or performance choices that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. For movement or instruments, use a clear space, ask an adult to be nearby and stop if anything feels unsafe. You may always describe a choice instead of performing it. One deliberate artistic choice with a named effect is more useful than a longer praise sentence.

teaching.model: At the end of a drama unit, students share their best scene and reflect on what they learned. A performance review looks at role, voice, body, use of space, props and audience connection. Give feedback as two stars, which are things that worked well, and a wish, which is one change. A reflection names what you did well, what was challenging and what you will practise next. Treat every performer with respect, and speak about the performance rather than the person. Now choose a different subject or piece to show you can transfer the idea.
teaching.rule: Use the same arts idea in a new artwork, song, drama or dance, not a copy of the example. Review clarity, safety and respectful practice.
teaching.why: This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.
